newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Bufori roadster taken for a second spin.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bufori roadster taken for a second spin.

text.p: It looks like a classic American or European car but is, in fact, an Australian creation. It runs on a Japanese engine and its manufacturers are officially Malaysian.

The Bufori, an antique-styled roadster with a modern powerplant, is being repackaged for an international launch later this year after failing to make much headway in Malaysia, where it was unveiled last year.
Kuala Lumpur-based STI Corp, which assembles the car, is confident the Bufori can compete with the Bentleys and BMWs of this world given its classic sporty look and performance.

"We're working on a V-6 model and talking to some American and British companies for the engine," Vinod Shekar, chief executive of STI, told Reuters in a recent interview. The Bufori was originally launched with 2.2 litre engine.
But auto analysts appeared generally unconvinced by the claims of the 28-year-old, self-described car nut, with a penchant for Mickey Mouse watches and clothes.
"They're going to need a super salesman for this car to create the kind of exclusivity that, let's say, the Mercedes SLK has," said Loke Chee Kien, auto analyst at Jupiter Securities.

Shekar spotted the Bufori during a trip to Australia in 1993 and a quick deal transferred the car's rights from a small factory run by the Khouri family in Sydney to STI's headquarters in Kuala Lumpur.
Bufori inventor Jerry Khouri came to work for STI and Japan's Subaru was enlisted to design a 2.2 litre engine.
Malaysian newspapers, sizing up the potential of the car after the nation's successful home-made sedan the Proton, gave the Bufori fair mileage in terms of publicity.
But a high-octane ad campaign hit a few potholes when one was withdrawn after women's organisations complained.
The model said in one ad she didn't care about the men in her life but "as long as you drive a Bufori, I'm yours".
But since the much-hyped launch last year by Malaysian King Tuanku Ja'afar Abdul Rahman, the Bufori has been practically running on empty.
"We sold about 60 units to local customers but couldn't deliver because we hadn't got government clearance for our prices," Shekar said.
"The biggest problem so far has been red tape," said Khouri, who invented the car in 1986. "We got our manufacturing licence and other specifications only approved last month."
Some $16 million had gone into research and development and other costs and about 70 percent of the components in the redesigned car would be Malaysian-made, said Shekar.
The first of the relaunched 2.2-litre series will roll out before year end at the old price -- 160,000 ringgit ($64,000).

A sneak preview of the restyled car showed little change from its old look. The walnut dashboard still has standard fuel, speed and temperature gauges. It sports leather seats, a huge air-conditioner unit and a compact-disc player.
The V-6 model, to roll out in about 15 months, will cost around 250,000 to 300,000 ringgit.
"At this price, I'd rather buy a BMW," said Kevin Chew, an analyst with research house Caspian. "The design may be classic but if I want vintage, I'd rather buy real vintage."
STI has projected a turnover of 21 million ringgit from Bufori's sales in 1997 and about 45 million in 1998. Shekar envisages a profit margin of "about 30 percent".
The company only plans to make 150 cars a year gradually building up to plant capacity of 800. All the parts are hand-tooled, Shekar said.
He rejected criticism that the Bufori did not offer value for money and could not be considered Malaysian.
"This car is in an incomparable class. It's a fun car and it's meant to be different," said Shekar.
"It'll always be known as Malaysian-grown", he said. "Yes, we took the body from Australia but we put it together here."
